questions.question: Which of the following is the best example of a carnivore?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **carnivore** is a biological organism that primarily derives its energy and nutrient requirements from a diet consisting of **animal tissue**, whether through predation or scavenging.
 
• The **Lion** (Panthera leo) is a quintessential example of an **obligate carnivore**, meaning its biological system is physically adapted to require nutrients found only in animal flesh.
 
• Lions function as **apex predators** in their ecosystems, predominantly the **African savannas** and the Gir Forest in India, where they regulate the populations of large ungulates.
 
• Scientific studies of their anatomy reveal specialized **carnassial teeth** and powerful jaws designed for shearing meat, alongside a relatively **short digestive tract** optimized for rapid protein absorption.
 
• In the **trophic level** hierarchy, lions occupy the position of **secondary or tertiary consumers**, playing a vital role in maintaining the **ecological balance** of their habitats.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dietary Classifications of Other Options**:

 
 
• **Herbivores**: Organisms like the **Cow** feed exclusively on plants. They possess complex **ruminant stomachs** and flat teeth designed for grinding **cellulose**.
 
• **Omnivores**: Animals like the **Crow** have a diverse diet including both plant matter (seeds, fruits) and animal matter (insects, small rodents), allowing them to adapt to various **biomes**.
 
• **Parasites**: The **Tapeworm** is an endoparasite that lives within the **intestines** of a host. Unlike carnivores that hunt and consume prey, parasites absorb **pre-digested nutrients** directly from the host organism.
 
 
 
• **Ecological Importance**:
 
 
• Carnivores prevent **overgrazing** by controlling the density of **primary consumers**, which in turn protects the **vegetation cover** and biodiversity of the region.

questions.question: Which structure in Agra Fort is characterized by its white marble arches and was used by Shah Jahan to view the Taj Mahal?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Musamman Burj**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Musamman Burj**, also known as the **Saman Burj** or **Shah-burj**, is a magnificent **octagonal tower** situated within the **Agra Fort** complex in **Uttar Pradesh**.
 
• Built by the Mughal Emperor **Shah Jahan** between **1631 and 1640**, the structure was originally intended for his wife, **Mumtaz Mahal**, and is celebrated for its **white marble arches** and **Pietra Dura** inlay work.
 
• The tower is strategically positioned on the riverfront, offering a panoramic and unobstructed view of the **Taj Mahal** across the **Yamuna River**.
 
• Historically, this structure is significant as the place where **Shah Jahan** was imprisoned by his son **Aurangzeb** for the last eight years of his life, during which he gazed at the **Taj Mahal** until his death in **1666**.
 
• The pavilion features a sunken **fountain** in the shape of a lotus and is surrounded by a **verandah** with beautiful **lattice screens** (Jalis) carved from marble.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Moti Masjid**:

 
 
• Commonly referred to as the **Pearl Mosque**, it was constructed by **Shah Jahan** for the royal court and is situated near the **Diwan-i-Aam**.
 
 
 
• **Nagina Masjid**:
 
 
• A small, private mosque built in **white marble** for the ladies of the **Zenana** (royal harem), known for its architectural simplicity and elegance.
 
 
 
• **Diwan-i-Khas**:
 
 
• The **Hall of Private Audience**, where the emperor held meetings with **high-ranking officials** and **dignitaries**, featuring the famous **Pachisi Court** and the **Takht-i-Taus** (Peacock Throne) base.

questions.question: The splitting of white light into colors was first explained by:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Isaac Newton**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In **1666**, the English scientist **Sir Isaac Newton** performed a landmark experiment using a **glass prism** to investigate the nature of light.
 
• He observed that when a narrow beam of sunlight (white light) passed through the prism, it spread out into a multi-colored band called a **spectrum**.
 
• This phenomenon is known as **dispersion**, which occurs because white light is a mixture of different colors that travel at different speeds through the glass.
 
• Newton identified the seven constituent colors as **Red**, **Orange**, **Yellow**, **Green**, **Blue**, **Indigo**, and **Violet**, often abbreviated as **VIBGYOR**.
 
• He proved that the prism was not coloring the light by using a **second inverted prism** to recombine the colored rays back into a single beam of **white light**.
 
• The experiment concluded that **refraction** depends on the wavelength; **violet light** has a shorter wavelength and bends the most, while **red light** has a longer wavelength and bends the least.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Thomas Young**:

 
 
• Famous for the **Double-Slit Experiment** conducted in **1801**.
 
• He demonstrated the **interference** of light, which provided critical evidence for the **wave theory of light**.
 
 
 
• **Christiaan Huygens**:
 
 
• A Dutch physicist who proposed the **wave theory of light** in **1678**.
 
• He developed the **Huygens-Fresnel principle**, explaining how **wavefronts** propagate through space.
 
 
 
• **James Clerk Maxwell**:
 
 
• Formulated the **Maxwell equations** in the **1860s**, unifying electricity and magnetism.
 
• He mathematically proved that light is an **electromagnetic wave** that travels at the speed of light.

questions.question: By how much was the Indian rupee devalued in July 1991 to tackle the balance of payments crisis?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**18-20%**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In **July 1991**, India faced a severe **Balance of Payments (BoP) crisis**, where foreign exchange reserves had dropped to approximately 1.2 billion dollars, barely enough to sustain two weeks of essential imports.
 
• The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** intervened by devaluing the **Indian Rupee** in two sharp steps to restore economic stability and international confidence.
 
• The first downward adjustment occurred on **July 1, 1991**, when the value of the rupee was reduced by about **9%** against major international currencies.
 
• The second adjustment followed quickly on **July 3, 1991**, with a further devaluation of about **11%**, bringing the cumulative devaluation to the range of **18-20%**.
 
• The primary objective of this **exchange rate adjustment** was to make **Indian exports** cheaper and more competitive globally while making **imports** more expensive to curb the widening trade deficit.
 
• This measure was a critical component of the structural adjustment program required to secure emergency assistance from the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** and the **World Bank**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Balance of Payments (BoP) Crisis of 1991**:

 
 
• The crisis was exacerbated by the **Gulf War (1990-91)**, which caused a spike in **crude oil prices** and reduced inward **remittances** from the Middle East.
 
• High **fiscal deficits** and **external debt** throughout the 1980s had made the Indian economy vulnerable to external shocks.
 
 
 
• **New Economic Policy (NEP)**:
 
 
• The devaluation acted as a catalyst for the **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG)** reforms introduced under the leadership of Prime Minister **P.V. Narasimha Rao** and Finance Minister **Dr. Manmohan Singh**.
 
• These reforms dismantled the **License Raj**, reduced **import tariffs**, and opened the Indian economy to **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)**.
 
 
 
• **Evolution of Exchange Rate System**:
 
 
• Following the 1991 crisis, India moved from a **fixed exchange rate** regime to a **Liberalized Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS)** in 1992, and eventually to a **managed float system** where market forces largely determine the rupee's value.

questions.question: The EXIM Bank of India was set up in:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1982**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Export-Import Bank of India**, commonly known as **EXIM Bank**, is a specialized financial institution wholly owned by the **Government of India**.
 
• It was established under the **Export-Import Bank of India Act, 1981**, and commenced its operations in **January 1982** to facilitate international trade.
 
• The bank serves as the principal financial institution for coordinating the working of various entities engaged in financing **export and import** activities of goods and services.
 
• Its primary mandate is to provide financial assistance to Indian exporters and importers while promoting **foreign trade** through various innovative credit programs.
 
• The **EXIM Bank** functions under the administrative control of the **Ministry of Finance** and is headquartered in **Mumbai**, Maharashtra.
 
• It plays a pivotal role in the globalization of Indian business by providing **Lines of Credit (LOCs)** to foreign governments and financial institutions to support the export of Indian equipment and services.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **SIDBI (Small Industries Development Bank of India)**:

 
 
• Established in **1990** under an Act of the Indian Parliament.
 
• It acts as the principal financial institution for the **promotion, financing, and development** of the Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (**MSME**) sector.
 
 
 
• **NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development)**:
 
 
• Established on **July 12, 1982**, based on the recommendations of the **B. Sivaraman Committee**.
 
• It focuses on the development of the **rural economy** by providing credit and other facilities for agriculture and allied activities.
 
 
 
• **Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (ECGC)**:
 
 
• Established in **1957** to strengthen the **export promotion** drive by covering the risk of exports on credit.
 
• It provides **credit insurance** to exporters against losses in the export of goods and services.

questions.question: Copper reacts with moist carbon dioxide in the air, gradually losing its shiny brown surface and developing a:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Green coat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When **copper** is exposed to the atmosphere for a prolonged period, it undergoes a chemical reaction with **moist carbon dioxide** and **oxygen** in the air.
 
• The **shiny brown surface** of the copper metal reacts with these gases to form a layer of **basic copper carbonate**.
 
• Basic copper carbonate is a chemical mixture consisting of **copper carbonate** (CuCO₃) and **copper hydroxide** (Cu(OH)₂), which has a distinctive **pale green** color.
 
• The overall chemical reaction can be represented as: 2Cu + H₂O + CO₂ + O₂ → CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂.
 
• This process is a type of **corrosion** where the metal surface is oxidized, causing it to lose its luster and acquire a **green coat** that actually protects the underlying metal from further deep corrosion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Black coat**:

 
 
• Formed when copper is heated strongly in the presence of **oxygen**.
 
• The reaction results in the formation of **copper(II) oxide** (CuO), which is a black solid.
 
 
 
• **Silver Corrosion**:
 
 
• Silver items develop a **black coat** over time.
 
• This occurs because silver reacts with **hydrogen sulfide** (H₂S) present in the air to form **silver sulfide** (Ag₂S).
 
 
 
• **Iron Rusting**:
 
 
• Iron develops a **reddish-brown** flaky substance called **rust**.
 
• This is caused by the reaction of iron with **moisture** and **oxygen** to form hydrated **iron(III) oxide** (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O).
 
 
 
• **Patina**:
 
 
• The green layer on copper is often called a **patina** and is highly valued in architecture and art, such as on the **Statue of Liberty**.

questions.question: Which of the following is a flow variable?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**National income**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **flow variable** is an economic quantity that is measured over a **specific period of time**, such as a month, a quarter, or a **fiscal year**.
 
• **National income** represents the total value of all final goods and services produced by the normal residents of a country during an **accounting year** (usually from April 1 to March 31 in India).
 
• It is categorized as a flow because it reflects the **continuous generation** of value, wages, interest, and profits over a time interval rather than a static amount held at one moment.
 
• The measurement of **National income** involves calculating the **Net National Product at Factor Cost** (NNP at FC), which requires aggregating economic activities throughout the year.
 
• Other prominent examples of flow variables include **consumption**, **investment**, **interest on capital**, **exports**, and **Gross Domestic Product** (GDP).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Stock Variables** are quantities measured at a **particular point in time**, representing an accumulation of assets or liabilities at a specific date.

 
 
• **Money Supply**: This refers to the total volume of **monetary assets** (like currency and deposits) held by the public at a **specific moment**; it is a stock because it is measured as a balance on a given day.
 
• **Capital Stock**: This represents the total **physical assets**, including buildings, machinery, and equipment, available in an economy at a given instant; it is the result of accumulated **net investment** (a flow).
 
• **Foreign Exchange Reserves**: These are the **foreign assets**, gold, and **Special Drawing Rights** (SDRs) held by the **Reserve Bank of India** (RBI) at a specific point in time to maintain **liquidity** and stability in the currency market.

questions.question: In May 2025, which Indian state was officially declared as fully literate under the ULLAS programme?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mizoram**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mizoram** has officially achieved the status of being a **fully literate state** under the **ULLAS** (Understanding of Lifelong Learning for All in Society) initiative as of **May 2025**.
 
• The **ULLAS programme**, also known as the **New India Literacy Programme (NILP)**, is a **Centrally Sponsored Scheme** designed to provide education to non-literates aged **15 years and above** who missed out on formal schooling.
 
• The state reached this milestone by successfully conducting the **Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN)** assessment tests across all its districts, ensuring that learners acquired basic reading, writing, and numeracy skills.
 
• The implementation strategy in the state relied heavily on **volunteerism**, where students and **community members** served as teachers to help achieve the goal of **Jan Jan Sakshar** (Literacy for every person).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **ULLAS Initiative Details**:

 
 
• The scheme is aligned with the **National Education Policy (NEP) 2020** and is scheduled for implementation from **FY 2022 to 2027**.
 
• It focuses on five pillars: **Foundational Literacy and Numeracy**, **Critical Life Skills** (financial, digital, legal literacy), **Vocational Skills**, **Basic Education**, and **Continuing Education**.
 
• The **ULLAS Mobile App** serves as a digital gateway for learners and volunteers to register and access multilingual educational resources.
 
 
 
• **Mizoram Literacy Landscape**:
 
 
• Historically, **Mizoram** has consistently ranked among the top Indian states in literacy, following **Kerala**, with a **Census 2011** literacy rate of **91.33%**.
 
• The success of literacy drives in the state is often attributed to the strong influence of **civil society organizations** and local **community-led initiatives**.

questions.question: Who was considered as most notable of the nine luminaries (navaratna) in Chandragupta II's court?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kalidas**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chandragupta II**, popularly known as **Vikramaditya**, was one of the most powerful emperors of the **Gupta Empire**, ruling from approximately **375 to 415 CE**.
 
• His court was renowned for the **Navaratnas** or **Nine Gems**, a circle of nine distinguished scholars who represented the pinnacle of intellectual and cultural achievement during the **Golden Age of India**.
 
• **Kalidas** is universally acknowledged as the most illustrious of these nine luminaries, celebrated as a master **Sanskrit** poet and playwright.
 
• His literary excellence earned him a legendary status in Indian history, with his works reflecting the sophisticated urban culture and religious synthesis of the **Gupta period**.
 
• His presence in the court of **Chandragupta II** highlights the royal patronage extended to the arts, which allowed classical **Sanskrit** literature to reach its zenith.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Works of Kalidas**:

 
 
• **Dramas**: His masterpiece is **Abhijnanashakuntalam**, which gained worldwide fame. Other significant plays include **Malavikagnimitram** and **Vikramorvasiyam**.
 
• **Epics**: He composed the great mahakavyas **Raghuvamsha** and **Kumarasambhava**.
 
• **Lyrics**: **Meghaduta** and **Ritusamhara** are his famous lyrical poems.
 
 
 
• **Context of Other Options**:
 
 
• **Tulsidas**: A saint-poet of the **Bhakti movement** who authored the **Ramcharitmanas** during the **16th century** (Mughal Era), long after the Gupta period.
 
• **Surdas**: A devotional singer and poet famous for **Sursagar**, who was a contemporary of the Mughal Emperor **Akbar** in the **16th century**.
 
• **Banabhatta**: The **Asthana Kavi** (court poet) of King **Harshavardhana** in the **7th century CE**, known for writing **Harshacharita** and **Kadambari**.

questions.question: Which of the following acts enacted in an effort to silence those newspapers that were critical of the government?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vernacular Press Act, 1878**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Vernacular Press Act** was enacted in **1878** during the viceroyalty of **Lord Lytton** to curtail the freedom of the Indian-language press and prevent the expression of criticism toward British policies. Hence, statement 1 is correct.
 
• The act was specifically designed to target **non-English publications**, providing the government with extensive powers to confiscate printing presses and editorial assets if they published 'seditious' material. Hence, statement 2 is incorrect as the act was passed in 1878, not 1858.
 
• The legislation was modeled on the repressive **Irish Press Laws** and was notoriously referred to as the **'Gagging Act'** because it discriminated between the English and the vernacular press.
 
• Under this law, a **District Magistrate** was empowered to call upon the printer and publisher of any vernacular newspaper to enter into a bond undertaking not to cause disaffection against the government.
 
• The **Amrita Bazar Patrika**, a prominent newspaper of the time, famously changed its language from Bengali to **English** overnight to circumvent the restrictions imposed by this act.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Charter Act, 1833**:

 
 
• It redesignated the **Governor-General of Bengal** as the **Governor-General of India**, with **Lord William Bentinck** becoming the first to hold this title.
 
• The act ended the **East India Company's** commercial privileges, transforming it into a purely administrative body under the British Crown.
 
 
 
• **Charter Act, 1813**:
 
 
• It abolished the trade monopoly of the **East India Company** in India, although the monopoly over trade in **tea** and trade with **China** was maintained.
 
• The act provided for a financial grant of **one lakh rupees** annually for the revival of Indian literature and the promotion of **scientific knowledge**.
 
 
 
• **Repeal of the Press Act**:
 
 
• The restrictive **Vernacular Press Act** was eventually repealed in **1882** by **Lord Ripon**, who is often remembered for his liberal reforms and for restoring the freedom of the press in India.

questions.question: In January 2025, Mantralaya's security was upgraded with facial recognition, RFID cards, and time-slot based visitor entry. In which state is this mantralaya located?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Maharashtra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The term **Mantralaya** refers to the administrative headquarters and the **State Secretariat** of the **Government of Maharashtra**, located in the **Nariman Point** area of **Mumbai**.
 
• In **January 2025**, the state government implemented a sophisticated security infrastructure to manage the daily influx of nearly **5,000 to 10,000 visitors** and prevent unauthorized access.
 
• The upgrade features **Facial Recognition Technology (FRT)**, which uses high-resolution cameras to capture and verify the identities of individuals entering the premises against a central database.
 
• The introduction of **RFID (Radio Frequency Identification)** cards for employees and permanent staff allows for automated, contact-free movement through specialized security turnstiles.
 
• To mitigate overcrowding and improve public service efficiency, a **time-slot based entry system** was integrated, requiring visitors to book appointments or receive digital tokens with specific arrival times.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Administrative Importance of Mantralaya**:

 
 
• The seven-story building houses the vital offices of the **Chief Minister**, **Deputy Chief Minister**, and **Chief Secretary** of Maharashtra.
 
• It was built in **1955** and was formerly known as **Sachivalaya** before being renamed to **Mantralaya** in **1980** to reflect the presence of the **Council of Ministers**.
 
• The **Home Department** of Maharashtra is responsible for the overall surveillance and protocol management of the complex.
 
• Following a major fire incident in **2012**, the building underwent extensive structural renovations, which paved the way for modernizing its **fire safety** and **digital security** protocols.

questions.question: The average number of children a woman expected to give birth during her life was 3.8 in ______ in India.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1990**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Total Fertility Rate (TFR)** represents the average number of children that would be born to a woman over her lifetime if she were to experience the prevailing age-specific fertility rates.
 
• In **1990**, India recorded a **Total Fertility Rate** of approximately **3.8 children per woman**, reflecting a significant phase in the nation's **demographic transition**.
 
• This period was characterized by a gradual shift from high birth rates to moderate levels due to increased awareness of **family planning** and improved **maternal healthcare** services.
 
• The 1990 figure of **3.8** served as a crucial benchmark in tracking India's progress toward achieving **Replacement Level Fertility**.
 
• Data from **international organizations** like the **World Bank** and India's **Sample Registration System (SRS)** confirm that the TFR hovered around this value during the late **1980s** and early **1990s**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Evolution of India's Fertility Rate**:

 
 
• **1960**: During this era, India had a very high **Total Fertility Rate**, estimated at nearly **5.9 children per woman**, as the country was in the early stage of the demographic transition.
 
• **2011**: By the time of the **2011 Census**, the fertility rate had dropped significantly to approximately **2.4 children per woman**.
 
• **2015**: According to the **National Family Health Survey-4 (NFHS-4)** conducted around 2015-16, the TFR was recorded at **2.2**, showing a steady decline toward the **replacement level**.
 
• **Replacement Level Fertility**: This is defined as the level of fertility (typically **2.1 children per woman**) at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next without migration.
 
• **Current Status**: According to **NFHS-5 (2019-21)**, India's overall TFR has further declined to **2.0**, which is below the replacement level of **2.1**.

questions.question: Tachi-Waza, Koshi-Waza are the term related to which of the following sports?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Judo**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Judo** is a modern **Japanese martial art** and combat sport created by **Kano Jigoro** in **1882**, which emphasizes the use of an opponent's force against themselves.
 
• The term **Tachi-Waza** refers to **Standing Techniques**. It is the broad category of throwing techniques performed while the practitioner is in a standing position.
 
• **Koshi-Waza** is a specialized sub-category of **Tachi-Waza** that specifically denotes **Hip Techniques**. These involve using the hip as a pivot or fulcrum to throw an opponent.
 
• The classification of these moves is part of the **Gokyo no Waza**, the standard syllabus of throwing techniques in **Kodokan Judo**.
 
• In a competitive **Judo** match, executing these techniques with speed, force, and control on the back can result in an **Ippon**, which grants an immediate victory.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nage-Waza (Throwing Techniques):**

 
 
• **Te-Waza:** Hand techniques where the arms and shoulders are the primary tools for the throw (e.g., **Seoi-nage**).
 
• **Ashi-Waza:** Foot and leg techniques used to trip or sweep the opponent (e.g., **Osoto-gari**).
 
• **Sutemi-Waza:** Sacrifice techniques where the practitioner falls to the ground to complete the throw.
 
 
 
• **Katame-Waza (Grappling Techniques):**
 
 
• **Osaekomi-Waza:** Pinning or holding techniques used to immobilize the opponent on their back.
 
• **Shime-Waza:** Choking or strangulation techniques applied to the neck.
 
• **Kansetsu-Waza:** Joint lock techniques, primarily targeting the elbow in **Judo** competition.
 
 
 
• **International Governing Body:**
 
 
• The **International Judo Federation (IJF)** manages international competitions and was established in **July 1951**.
 
• **Judo** made its **Olympic Games** debut for men at the **1964 Tokyo Olympics** and for women at the **1992 Barcelona Olympics**.

questions.question:
Which of the following pair of component - process regarding water cycle is correct?

I. Water storage in ice and snow - Evapotranspiration 

II. Groundwater storage - Groundwater discharge springs
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Water storage in ice and snow** refers to the accumulation of frozen freshwater in **glaciers**, **ice caps**, and permanent snowfields. **Evapotranspiration** is the collective process of **evaporation** from surfaces and **transpiration** from plants, primarily involving liquid water and biological activity. The direct transition of ice or snow into water vapor is known as **sublimation**, not evapotranspiration. ***Hence, statement I is incorrect.***
 
• **Groundwater storage** constitutes the water located beneath the Earth's surface in soil pore spaces and the fractures of rock formations, known as **aquifers**. **Groundwater discharge** occurs when this subsurface water moves toward the surface; **springs** are the natural locations where this stored water flows out onto the land or into water bodies. ***Hence, statement II is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hydrological Cycle Components**:

 
 
• **Sublimation**: This process allows **ice and snow** to enter the atmosphere as vapor without melting into liquid water first. It is a critical factor in the mass balance of **glaciers**.
 
• **Transpiration**: The process by which moisture is carried through plants from roots to small pores on the underside of leaves, where it changes to vapor and is released to the atmosphere.
 
• **Aquifers**: These are permeable layers of **sediment** or **rock** that act as underground reservoirs. They are replenished through **infiltration** and **percolation**.
 
• **Water Table**: The upper surface of the **zone of saturation**, where the pressure of groundwater is equal to atmospheric pressure. When the water table meets the land surface, a **spring** or **wetland** is formed.
